brief.topic: How to write acceptance criteria for an AI feature that will sometimes be wrong
brief.audience: PMs moving into AI product management and product leaders writing PRDs for GenAI features
constraints: Illustrative numbers labelled on screen and in caption

coreInsight: Acceptance criteria for an AI feature must define how often it may fail, which failures are never acceptable, what users see when it’s unsure, and its cost and latency ceiling.

hooks.text: Your AI feature will be wrong. Spec for it.
hooks.notes: Reframes failure as a design requirement; immediately clear; the framework delivers on it.

hooks.text: “It works” is not an acceptance criterion for AI.
hooks.notes: Strong, but sounds like a scolding and doesn't hint at the fix.

hooks.text: Four numbers every AI PRD needs before launch.
hooks.notes: Useful but generic; 'numbers' undersells the failure-budget idea.

selectionRationale: Highest total (24/25). It states an uncomfortable truth every AI PM recognises and turns it into a concrete instruction the reel then delivers as a four-part framework.

scenes.purpose: Make the viewer accept that failure is certain, so specifying it feels necessary rather than pessimistic.
scenes.onScreen: Your AI feature will be wrong. Spec for it. / 4 acceptance criteria that do.
scenes.voiceover: Your AI feature will be wrong sometimes. So write that into the spec.

storyboard.visual: Four-line display headline, 'Spec for it.' in cyan with indigo underline; slate sub-line.
storyboard.animation: Headline readable on frame 0; underline sweeps from frame 6; sub-line rises at 18.

scenes.purpose: Deliver the framework: the four criteria a probabilistic feature needs, plus the decision rule.
scenes.onScreen: THE FRAMEWORK / Acceptance criteria for AI features / 1 Quality bar 2 Failure budget 3 Fallback 4 Cost & latency ceiling / Ship only when all four have a number and an owner.
scenes.voiceover: Four criteria. A quality bar on a fixed eval set. A failure budget: which errors are never acceptable. A fallback: what users see when the model is unsure. And a cost and latency ceiling. Ship only when each has a number and an owner.

storyboard.visual: Kicker + two-line headline. Four numbered rows with indigo number badges. Cyan-outlined decision rule box below.
storyboard.animation: Items rise every 42 frames from frame 24 with badge pop; rule rises at 198; ~3.4s hold.

items: Quality bar: ≥ X% pass on a fixed eval set
Failure budget: errors that are never OK
Fallback: what users see when it’s unsure
Ceiling: max cost and latency per request
scenes.rule: Ship only when all four have a number and an owner.

scenes.purpose: Make the framework concrete with a labelled illustrative example the viewer can copy.
scenes.onScreen: EXAMPLE · ILLUSTRATIVE / Invoice-extraction assistant / QUALITY BAR ≥95% correct on 200 test docs / NEVER OK Wrong bank account number / FALLBACK Unsure? Flag for human review / CEILING Under 4 s, $0.02 per invoice
scenes.voiceover: For example, an invoice-extraction assistant: ninety-five percent correct on two hundred test documents. Never a wrong bank account number. When unsure, flag for human review. Under four seconds and two cents per invoice. These numbers are illustrative.

storyboard.visual: Kicker carries the ILLUSTRATIVE label. Four tagged cards: three green (quality, fallback, ceiling), one amber 'NEVER OK' card.
storyboard.animation: Cards rise every 30 frames from frame 10 with icon pop; ~4.5s hold for reading/screenshots.

scenes.purpose: Resolve the hook with a memorable rule and a save CTA.
scenes.onScreen: Write down how it fails, before launch. / Save this for your next AI PRD
scenes.voiceover: Write down how it fails, before launch. Save this for your next AI PRD.

storyboard.animation: Lines rise with 6-frame stagger; CTA at 40; end card at 70; static final frame.

caption.opening: “It works” is not an acceptance criterion for a feature that is right most of the time.
body:
For an AI feature, acceptance criteria need four parts:
→ Quality bar: a pass rate on a fixed eval set
→ Failure budget: the errors that are never acceptable
→ Fallback: what users see when the model is unsure
→ Ceiling: maximum cost and latency per request
If any of the four is missing a number or an owner, the launch decision becomes a debate about vibes.
(The invoice example numbers in the reel are illustrative, not from a real product.)

claims.text: Acceptance criteria for probabilistic features should specify a quality bar, a failure budget, fallback behaviour and cost/latency ceilings.
Invoice example: ≥95% on 200 docs, never a wrong bank account, flag when unsure, <4 s and <$0.02 per invoice.
